title: Business training, data science tools.
text:
About
    Business training, data science tools.
    I started out as an accounting major at the University of Ottawa, quickly realized it wasn’t for me, and switched to business technology management. Then I spent two years at the Department of National Defence turning SAP and CRM data into dashboards and automations people actually used.
    That work showed me how much a good question and clean data matter. I came to Georgetown for the statistics and machine learning, and now I build data pipelines and dashboards for the School of Medicine. In between, I automated subscription and newsletter reporting at AL-Monitor.
    I like problems where the hard part is getting the data right: reconciling sources that don’t agree, catching the records a report silently drops, and turning the result into something a busy person can read in a minute.
    Outside of data, I love horse riding. Every new place I visit, I try to find a ranch and take the horses out for a ride.

title: Woof Woof: a dog adoption app
text: This interactive Python application, built in Jupyter Notebook, demonstrates fundamental programming concepts through a practical dog adoption and services platform. The application features user authentication, search functionality, and a dynamic booking system for various dog-related services.

title: Woof Woof: a dog adoption app
text:
Part 1: Basic Authentication and Search

User Login System
The first iteration implements a basic login system using lists to store usernames and passwords.

# Login function
user_name = ['vbrad','nokwe','dadel','hjami']
user_password = ['brad123','okwe123','johnhancock1977','jami1234']

login_username = input("Enter your username (Note: Case Sensitive): ")
login_password = input("Enter your password (Note: Case Sensitive): ")

# For loop to login
for n in user_name and user_password:
  if login_username in user_name and login_password in user_password:
    print("Login Successful")
    break
  else:
    print("Username or Password is wrong, Try again")
    break



Service Search Functionality
Users can search for available services using partial matching with the startswith() method and in operator.

stuff = ["Adopt a Dog", "Foster a Dog ", "Donate a Dog", "Dog Therapy",
         "Dog Yoga ", "Dog Training", "Dog Grooming","Dog Recipes"]

print("Welcome to Woof Woof, a one stop for all things dogs!")

search_function = input("What Service are you looking for today: ")
search_function = search_function.lower()

options_list = []

# Using a for loop to search for a partial match in the list
for s in stuff:
  s = s.lower()
  m = s.startswith((search_function))
  if m == True or search_function in s:
    options_list.append(s)



Displaying Search Results

# Check if anything was found
if options_list == []:
  print(f"No results found with search")
else:
    print(f"Here are results that match your search:")
    for index, op in enumerate(options_list):
        new_index = index + 1
        print(f"{new_index}. {op}")

    num_stuff_selec = int(input("Select an option from the list: "))
    new_num_stuff_selec = int(num_stuff_selec) - 1

    if new_num_stuff_selec >= 0 and new_num_stuff_selec < len(options_list):
        print(f'You have chosen {num_stuff_selec} and want to view {options_list[new_num_stuff_selec]}')
    else:
        print(f'You have entered {num_stuff_selec}, which is not on the list.')

title: Woof Woof: a dog adoption app
section: Part 2: Enhanced Application with Dictionary-Based Data Structures
text:
Part 2: Enhanced Application with Dictionary-Based Data Structures

User Authentication with Dictionaries
The enhanced version uses nested dictionaries for more robust user authentication, mapping usernames to user details.

user_details = {
    'vbrad': {'firstname':'valerie', 'lastname': 'bradley', 'password': 'brad123'},
    'nokwe': {'firstname':'nkemdibe', 'lastname': 'okweye', 'password': 'okwe123'},
    'dadel': {'firstname':'daniel', 'lastname': 'adelberg', 'password': 'johnhancock1977'},
    'hjami': {'firstname':'hisham', 'lastname': 'jamil', 'password': 'jami1234'}
}



Dog Database Structure
A comprehensive database tracks dog information including breed, gender, age, availability status, and attributes.

dog_database = {
    'luna': {'breed':'husky', 'gender':'female', 'age': '12 months',
             'status': 'available','attribute': 'good with kids'},
    'rex': {'breed':'german shepherd', 'gender':'male', 'age': '6 months',
            'status': 'available','attribute': 'good around other dogs'},
    'prince': {'breed':'doberman', 'gender':'male', 'age': '2 years',
               'status': 'unavailable','attribute': 'friendly'},
    'daisy': {'breed':'goldendoodle', 'gender':'male', 'age': '2 years',
              'status': 'available','attribute': 'energetic'},
    'koda': {'breed':'samoyed', 'gender':'female', 'age': '4 months',
             'status': 'unavailable','attribute': 'playful'},
    'mona': {'breed':'husky', 'gender':'female', 'age': '7 months',
             'status': 'available','attribute': 'nice'},
    'lola': {'breed':'dalmation', 'gender':'female', 'age': '2 months',
             'status': 'available','attribute': 'protective'}
}



Enhanced Login and Service Selection

stuff = ["Adopt a Dog", "Foster a Dog ", "Dog Therapy", "Dog Yoga ",
         "Dog Training", "Dog Grooming"]

options_list, avail_dog_database = [], []

# Check if the user's name matches their password
login_user = input("Enter your username (Note: Case Sensitive): ")
login_pass = input("Enter your password (Note: Case Sensitive): ")

for user in user_details:
  if login_user in user_details and login_pass == user_details[login_user]['password']:
    print("Login Successful")

    print(f"Welcome {user_details[login_user]['firstname']} {user_details[login_user]['lastname']} to Woof Woof, a one-stop for all things dogs!")
    search_function = input("What Service are you looking for today: ")
    search_function = search_function.lower()

    # Search for matching services
    for s in stuff:
      s = s.lower()
      m = s.startswith((search_function))
      if m == True or search_function in s:
        options_list.append(s)
        continue

    if options_list != []:
      print(f"Here are results that match your search:")

      for index, op in enumerate(options_list):
        new_index = index + 1
        print(f"{new_index}. {op}")

      num_stuff_selec = int(input("Select an option from the list: "))
      new_num_stuff_selec = int(num_stuff_selec) - 1

      # Check if the number entered is valid
      if new_num_stuff_selec >= 0 and new_num_stuff_selec < len(options_list):
        print(f'You have chosen {num_stuff_selec} and want to view {options_list[new_num_stuff_selec]}')

        print(f'Here are the dogs available:')
        for dog in dog_database:
          if dog_database[dog]['status'] == 'available':
            avail_dog_database.append(dog)
      else:
        print(f'You have entered {num_stuff_selec}, which is not on the list.')
        break
    else:
      print(f"No results found with search")
  else:
    print("Username or Password is wrong, Try again")
  break



Dog Adoption Process
This section handles the complete adoption workflow, including selection, confirmation, and status updates.

if avail_dog_database != [] and options_list[new_num_stuff_selec] == "adopt a dog":
  for i, adog in enumerate(avail_dog_database):
    new_i = i + 1
    print(f"{new_i}. {adog}, {dog_database[adog]['breed']}, {dog_database[adog]['gender']}, {dog_database[adog]['age']}, {dog_database[adog]['attribute']}")

  num_avail_dog = int(input("Select a dog from the list: "))
  new_num_avail_dog = int(num_avail_dog) - 1

  if new_num_avail_dog >= 0 and new_num_avail_dog < len(avail_dog_database):
    print(f'You have chosen {avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]}')

    adopt_choice = input("Enter Yes to confirm adoptions and No to cancel: ")
    adopt_choice = adopt_choice.lower()

    if adopt_choice == "yes":
      dog_database[avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]]['status']='unavailable'

      print(f'Your adoption process of {avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]} is complete')
      print(f"{avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]} status has now been updated to {dog_database[avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]]['status']}")
    else:
      print(f'Your adoption process of {avail_dog_database[new_num_avail_dog]} was not complete')
  else:
    print(f'You have entered {num_avail_dog}, which is not on the list')



Other Services Booking
This section manages bookings for services like therapy, yoga, training, and grooming.

if avail_dog_database != [] and options_list[new_num_stuff_selec] != "adopt a dog":
    for i, adog in enumerate(avail_dog_database):
        print(f"{i+1}. {adog}, {dog_database[adog]['breed']}, {dog_database[adog]['gender']}, {dog_database[adog]['age']}, {dog_database[adog]['attribute']}")

    num_service_dog = int(input("Select a dog from the list for the service: "))
    new_num_service_dog = num_service_dog - 1

    if new_num_service_dog >= 0 and new_num_service_dog < len(avail_dog_database):
        selected_dog = avail_dog_database[new_num_service_dog]
        print(f'You have chosen {selected_dog} for {options_list[new_num_stuff_selec]}.')

        confirm_choice = input("Enter Yes to confirm and No to cancel: ").lower()
        if confirm_choice == "yes":
            dog_database[selected_dog]['status'] = 'unavailable'
            print(f'{selected_dog} has been booked for {options_list[new_num_stuff_selec]}.')
            print(f"{avail_dog_database[new_num_service_dog]} status has now been updated to {dog_database[avail_dog_database[new_num_service_dog]]['status']}")
        else:
            print(f'Your booking of {selected_dog} for {options_list[new_num_stuff_selec]} was not complete.')
    else:
        print(f'You have entered {num_service_dog}, which is not on the list.')

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
TeamPavlos Baffes, Noelle Martell, Younghoon Kim, Nkem Okweye, Nikhil Patla
  CourseDSAN 5100, Probabilistic Modeling & Statistical Computing
  Data23 elections · 6 states · 1980–2024
  ToolsR, Python, Quarto

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
The question
Turnout swings a lot between states and elections. We asked whether the conditions people live with, such as unemployment, housing costs, crime and cost of living, predict participation better than civic duty alone.

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
Data
Turnout from the University of Florida Election Lab, joined with FRED economic series (unemployment, median household income, housing price index), FBI violent-crime rates, NOAA Election Day weather and U.S. Census population, for New York, California, Ohio, Michigan, Florida and Utah.

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
Method
one-way ANOVAWelch’s ANOVAchi-squarepermutation testsbootstrapARIMABonferroniGames-Howell
We checked assumptions with Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s tests before each comparison, and used post-hoc procedures across 12+ hypothesis tests. ARIMA models forecast 2026 unemployment for Florida, California and Michigan.

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
Results

  +5.47pts turnout, swing vs. blue states (presidential)p = 0.0012
  ~5pts higher presidential turnout in high-HPI statesp = 0.0007
  +4.35pts, medium- vs. high-crime electionsp = 0.004

Weather had no significant effect on turnout, and all three forecast states point to rising unemployment going into the 2026 midterms.

title: What actually drives Americans to vote?
text:
What it means
Turnout responds to the conditions voters live in, not only to partisanship. Campaigns can use local economic conditions to understand which issues will move people to vote.

title: The Menendez Brothers, from courtroom to comments section
text:
The question
In 1989 Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents in Beverly Hills. Coverage moved from tabloid sensation to a Netflix-era reappraisal of abuse and justice. I measured how that narrative changed across three decades and across platforms.

title: The Menendez Brothers, from courtroom to comments section
text:
Data
A pipeline pulling 2,840+ documents from the Guardian API, the YouTube Data API v3 and historical archives, cleaned through a repeatable ETL workflow.

title: The Menendez Brothers, from courtroom to comments section
text:
Method
TF-IDFMultinomial Naive Bayeslogistic regressionK-MeansPCAt-SNEsentiment analysis
Supervised models classified documents by source and era, tuned with hyperparameter search and feature selection. Unsupervised methods reduced 2,000+ TF-IDF features into three interpretable narrative clusters.

title: The Menendez Brothers, from courtroom to comments section
text:
Results

  96.8%test accuracy after tuningMultinomial Naive Bayes
  3distinct narrative clusters from 2,000+ featuresK-Means + t-SNE
  0.4point sentiment gap, journalism vs. social mediasentiment model

title: The Menendez Brothers, from courtroom to comments section
text:
What it means
Traditional journalism and social media tell measurably different stories about the same case. The clusters trace the shift from tabloid framing toward conversations about abuse, male victimization and criminal-justice reform.

title: The Vanishing Entry Point
text:
The question
More people hold bachelor’s degrees than ever, yet new graduates say the first job is harder to land. We set out to check whether the data backs that up, using underemployment as the main lens: graduates working jobs that don’t typically need a degree.

title: The Vanishing Entry Point
text:
Data

BLS JOLTS: job openings, hires and layoffs, monthly, 2015–2025
NY Fed College Labor Market: unemployment and underemployment for recent grads aged 22–27, 1990–2025
NCES Digest of Education Statistics: bachelor’s degrees conferred, 1970–2021
Google Trends: six job-search terms such as “entry level jobs” and “years of experience required”, 2015–2025
Georgetown CEW + NY Fed Major Explorer: 74 majors matched after harmonizing names

title: The Vanishing Entry Point
text:
Method
D3.js bubble chartChart.js line & gap chartsannotation layerssource harmonizationscroll storytelling
We built the story as a single-page site with no frameworks: seven Chart.js charts, an interactive unemployment vs. underemployment toggle, and a D3 bubble chart where each major’s size is its early-career wage. Google Trends is used only as corroborating evidence, and we left sparse pre-2005 NCES years uninterpolated.

title: The Vanishing Entry Point
text:
Results

  46%fewer actual hires than job postings impliedBLS JOLTS
  ~42%of recent graduates are underemployedNY Fed
  1.07 → 1.75openings per hire, 2015 to the 2022 peakBLS JOLTS
  12.3Mjob openings in March 2022, the highest on recordBLS JOLTS

Bachelor’s completions more than doubled from 839K in 1970 to 2.07M in 2021. Underemployment for liberal arts and general business majors runs two to three times higher than for engineering and nursing.

title: The Vanishing Entry Point
text:
What it means
Postings overstated real demand. Openings surged after 2021 while hiring did not keep pace, so new graduates competed for fewer real jobs than the headlines suggested.
